strengths: Well-motivated problem analysis: Clear identification and articulation of why point-based drag methods fail on DiTs due to feature granularity differences, well-illustrated in Figure 2
Comprehensive technical approach: Addresses multiple challenges (region supervision, background preservation, subject consistency) with well-justified solutions
Thorough experimental validation: Extensive comparison against 9 baselines, evaluation on 2 benchmarks, multiple metrics, and ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution
Strong and consistent empirical results: Achieves best or competitive performance across all metrics on both DragBench-DR and ReD Bench with impressive qualitative results
New benchmark contribution: ReD Bench provides valuable region-level annotations with task tags and detailed descriptions, advancing evaluation methodology
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation details, clear hyperparameter specifications, promise to release code/datasets, comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: Region-based affine supervision is relatively straightforward; hard constraints are intuitive; adapter injection leverages existing IP-Adapter; MLLM task disambiguation is orthogonal. The contribution is primarily a combination and application rather than fundamental innovation

Narrow model-specific design: Method is specifically optimized for FLUX.1-dev; generalization to other DiTs is unclear. No evaluation on SD models or other DiT architectures to demonstrate broader applicability

Unresolved CFG-distillation limitation: Paper acknowledges but works around FLUX's inversion drift rather than solving it. IFbg ranks second due to inherent model limitations, suggesting adaptation to weakness rather than capability advancement

Incomplete baseline comparison: Most comparable baseline is RegionDrag (also region-based), but no experiment with RegionDrag using FLUX as base model. Unclear how much improvement comes from method vs. base model upgrade
User input burden underexplored: Both DragFlow and RegionDrag require manual source region specification; practical advantage over RegionDrag unclear. User study would strengthen usability claims
Missing computational analysis: No runtime comparison with baselines; unclear if 70 optimization iterations is practical for interactive editing; overhead of reconstruction branch not quantified
Insufficient failure analysis: Acknowledges 'detail loss in highly intricate structures' but provides no examples, quantitative analysis, or boundary case discussion
Evaluation metric limitations: Heavy reliance on LPIPS which has known limitations; no user study validation; no analysis of metric correlation with human preference
Orthogonal MLLM contribution: Task disambiguation via GPT-5 could be applied to other methods; contribution to results unclear; adds external dependency
ReD Bench scale: 120 images is relatively small for a benchmark; no inter-rater agreement analysis for annotations

Ranks second on IFbg metric despite background preservation claims; hard constraint approach requires additional reconstruction branch with unquantified overhead

strengths: Well-motivated problem diagnosis: Clear analysis of why point-based drag editing fails on DiTs due to feature granularity differences (Section 3.1, Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Two benchmarks, 9 baseline comparisons, thorough ablations (Table 3, Figure 6), and extensive supplementary analysis
New benchmark contribution: ReD Bench with region-level annotations, task labels, and contextual descriptions addresses limitations of point-based benchmarks
Strong qualitative results: Figure 5 and comparisons demonstrate clear improvements in reducing distortion artifacts on complex scenes
Reproducibility-focused: Detailed implementation details in appendices, code and dataset promised for release
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: The central contribution—replacing point supervision with region-level affine supervision—is straightforward once the problem is identified. Affine transformations and region-based matching are standard techniques, not novel

Over-engineered solution: The method combines region-level supervision, gradient masking, adapter-enhanced inversion, and MLLM-based intent parsing. Unclear which components are essential vs. optional enhancements; obscures the core contribution

Prohibitive computational cost: DragFlow requires 158.7 seconds vs. 5.4-113.2s for baselines with 23.5 GB peak memory. This 40%+ slowdown is inadequately justified for interactive editing, yet barely discussed in the paper

Heavy dependence on external GPT-5 API: Framework critically relies on proprietary GPT-5 for operation classification, prompt generation, and intent parsing. Raises serious reproducibility, accessibility, and reliability concerns. API changes could break the method

Unfair experimental comparison: Main results use FLUX.1 (stronger base model) while baselines use Stable Diffusion 1.5/2.0. All improvements could be attributed to superior base model. Fair comparison (Table 7, SD3.5) relegated to appendix with slightly lower performance

User input complexity understated: Paper claims only 'target points' needed but Section 3.2 requires users to draw source region masks. Sensitivity to mask quality (Figure 13) not quantified. More complex than claimed

Limited technical depth in individual components: Affine transformation is standard, gradient masking is well-known, IP-Adapter injection is existing technique, MLLM integration is straightforward. Contribution is primarily in combination, not innovation

Weak evaluation methodology: No user studies to validate practical utility; LPIPS/MD metrics have known limitations; Modified MD2 metric complicates future comparisons; ReD Bench is small (120 images); failure case analysis primarily anecdotal

Insufficient theoretical analysis: Why do affine transformations specifically solve DiT feature granularity? Why layers 17-18? Why are hard constraints necessary for DiTs but not UNets? Design principles lack depth

Generalization concerns: Method appears tailored specifically to DiT properties. Broader applicability across architectures unclear despite SD3.5 results. Scalability to complex multi-object scenes unaddressed

strengths: Well-motivated technical insight distinguishing DiT feature granularity from UNet bottlenecks, clearly explaining why point-based drag methods fail (Section 3.1, Figure 2)

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: 9 baselines, 2 benchmarks, multiple complementary metrics, thorough ablations (Table 3), layer-wise analysis of all 57 FLUX layers (Section C.5), cross-architecture validation (SD3.5)
Strong empirical results with clear improvements: best MD1 (31.59 vs 32.32), strong IFs2s (0.941), superior qualitative visual results (Figure 5)
Excellent reproducibility: promised code/dataset release, 100+ pages of implementation details, feature visualizations, dataset samples, comprehensive ablations

Well-justified technical solutions: region-level supervision aligns with DiT feature structure, hard constraints elegantly handle CFG-distillation without loss balancing, adapter-enhanced inversion shows clear improvement (Table 1)
Practical contributions: new ReD Bench with region-point alignment, adaptive multi-operation weighting, automatic mask generation, generalizes across DiT architectures
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-organized comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: region-based supervision exists (RegionDrag), affine transformations are standard, IP-Adapter usage is straightforward application; core contribution is combination for DiTs rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation
Significant computational overhead: 158.7s vs FastDrag's 5.4s (29× slower), 23.5GB vs RegionDrag's 4.3GB memory; severely limits practical interactive adoption despite acknowledgment in Table 6

Unfair model comparison: DragFlow uses FLUX (much larger, stronger prior) while all 9 baselines use Stable Diffusion; confounds method contribution with base model capacity; Table 7 shows advantage reduces when compared on SD3.5 (35.21 vs 32.32)
Heavy input quality dependency: empirical evidence (Section H.3) shows failure with undersized masks; relies on accurate target point specification; no systematic robustness analysis to imprecision
ReD Bench limitations: only 120 images, custom metrics lack standard validation, point-to-region alignment procedure underspecified, unclear generalization to diverse real-world scenarios

Incomplete analysis: no user studies on practical utility, limited theoretical justification beyond receptive field intuition, CFG-distillation challenges persist (IFbg not perfect), missing ablation comparing region supervision on SD-based methods

MLLM dependency concerns: uses GPT-5 with limited availability, external service dependency, prompts improve results (31.59 vs 33.81 MD1) contradicting robustness claims, double-confirmation workflow adds interaction burden
Limited scope of baseline comparisons: point-based methods (DragNoise, CLIPDrag) evaluated only on SD, not on FLUX where the method claims point-based approaches fail
